evidence: Plaut. Pers. 2.5.11: quid hoc hīc in collō tibi tumet?
terms.comment: Of a part of the body, a sponge, a bud, the sea. The perfect tumuī is that of tumēscō.

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica; not in Cicero

terms.comment: Lewis & Short give sē attollere as “to raise oneself, rise”, not of swelling; say tumēscere, and of swelling that goes down, dētumēscere.
Traupman’s phrase; we have found no classical instance of it for a swelling. Celsus says īnflammātiō conquiēscit (7.19, Lewis & Short s.v. conquiēscō).

phrases.latin: Quid hoc hīc in collō tibi tumet?
phrases.english: What’s this swelling here on your neck?

phrases.latin: haec tibi sorte datur tergendīs spongia mēnsīs ūtilis, expressō cum levis imbre tumet
phrases.english: this sponge falls to your lot, useful for wiping tables when, squeezed of its water, it swells up light
